unitObjectives.objective: Pupils will be able to ask and answer prices of classroom and everyday items using 'How much is it? / It is...'
Pupils will be able to identify 6 major historical stages of money on a chronological timeline (barter, shells, metal tools, coins, paper, credit cards).
Pupils will be able to identify problems and solutions in informational and narrative texts.
Pupils will be able to pronounce and spell words with the 'ar' pattern (/ɑːr/ sound: car, park, hard, farm, card).
Pupils will be able to express ethical choices using 'could' and 'should' regarding saving, spending, and helping family.
Pupils will be able to retell the story 'The $100 Bill' using a 5-step narrative frame.

I can tell the price of an item in dollars or liras.
I can name three things people used as money long ago.

I can say what I should do when money is tight.

reading.objective: Follow a chronological timeline and identify problem-solution text structures in fiction and nonfiction.

listening.objective: Listen to prices and narrative details to match items with their owners and historical dates.

speaking.objective: Ask and tell prices in a classroom shop role-play and discuss saving versus spending.

writing.objective: Write 3-4 sentences completing a Problem and Solution story map about saving money.

vocabulary.objective: Recognize, understand, and use 10 core words and idioms related to money and commerce.

grammar.objective: Use past simple verbs (-ed and irregular) and modals 'could' and 'should' for choices.

phonics.objective: Distinguish and pronounce the /ɑːr/ vowel sound in one-syllable and two-syllable words.

content.objective: Understand that money is an agreed tool that evolved to make trading easier.

thinking.objective: Sequence historical events in order of time and evaluate good financial decisions.

values.objective: Appreciate family effort, generosity over selfishness, and empathy when money is tight.

successCriteria.criterion: Pupil holds up an item and accurately asks 'How much is it?' during pair work.
Pupil places 'barter', 'shells', 'metal coins', and 'paper money' in correct chronological order on the smartboard.

grammar.form: How much is / are ___? -> It is / They are ___.
grammar.meaning: Asking and stating the cost of items.
grammar.use: Use 'is' for one item (singular) and 'are' for two or more items (plural).
grammar.simpleRule: Use 'is' for one thing, and 'are' for many things.
practiceSentences: How much is the toy car?

commonTurkishL1Errors.explanation: Turkish uses 'kaç' or 'ne kadar' interchangeably. Students mix up 'how much' (price/uncountable) and 'how many' (quantity).
Turkish word order causes students to omit question inversion (subject-verb inversion).

grammar.meaning: Expressing possibility (could) versus the best moral choice (should).
grammar.use: Use 'could' for options you have, and 'should' for what is right or best to do.
bookExamples: Paige could buy a new phone. (p.51)
What should she do with the money? (p.51)
grammar.simpleRule: 'Could' means you have a choice; 'should' means it is the kind, right thing to do.
practiceSentences: You could spend it or save it.
She should return the lost book.

commonTurkishL1Errors.error: She should to buy a phone.
commonTurkishL1Errors.explanation: Turkish learners often add 'to' after modal verbs (should to / could to).
Learners add third-person '-s' to the main verb after could/should.

grammar.form: Subject + Verb-ed / Irregular Past (bartered, started, found, saw)
grammar.meaning: Narrating events that happened and finished in the past.
grammar.use: Use past tense to tell historical facts and story events.
bookExamples: Thousands of years ago, people bartered. (p.42)
Paige found a $100 bill in the park. (p.50)
Dad smiled when the pizza arrived. (p.53)
grammar.simpleRule: Add -ed for yesterday's actions, or use special past words like found and saw.
practiceSentences: She put the bill in her pocket.

commonTurkishL1Errors.explanation: Turkish learners often drop past tense endings when time markers ('long ago') are present.
Overregularization of irregular past verbs (adding -ed to 'find').

readings.title: The History of Money
readings.mainIdea: Money evolved from bartering to shells, metal coins, paper notes, and electronic credit cards to make trade easier.
readings.summary: Thousands of years ago, people did not have money. When they needed food or tools, they bartered goods like grain and goats. Later, people used rare cowrie shells as money. In China, people made small metal knives and spades to trade. In Lydia around 600 BCE, people stamped pictures onto metal coins. Because heavy metal coins were hard to carry, paper money was invented in China. Today, people use plastic credit cards and computers to pay for things instantly.
keySentences: Thousands of years ago, people did not use money. They bartered. (p.42)
In China around 1000 BCE, people made small tools from metal to use as money. (p.43)
Today, people use plastic credit cards and computers to pay for things. (p.45)

characters.name: Ancient traders
characters.trait: Bartered grain and animals without coins

characters.name: Lydian coin makers
characters.trait: Stamped the first metal coins around 600 BCE

readings.setting: Ancient marketplaces (China, Lydia/Anatolia) to modern computerized stores
sequence: 1. 6000 BCE: People barter goods like wheat, goats, and cows.
2. 1200 BCE: People use rare cowrie shells as valuable money.
3. 1000 BCE: China makes metal spade and knife tools to trade.
4. 600 BCE: Lydia stamps pictures onto the first round metal coins.
5. 800-900 CE: China invents light paper money because coins are heavy.
6. 1958-Today: Credit cards and digital computer money are used worldwide.

problemSolution.problem: People did not always want what another person had to trade.
problemSolution.solution: People agreed on valuable standard items like cowrie shells and metal coins.

problemSolution.problem: Carrying thousands of heavy metal coins was difficult and dangerous for travelers.
problemSolution.solution: People invented light paper bills that were easy to carry in pockets.

readings.moralOrMessage: Inventions happen when people need to solve everyday problems and cooperate.

readings.title: The $100 Bill
readings.mainIdea: Making family happy and showing generosity is worth more than having expensive material gadgets.
readings.summary: Paige feels left out after school because her friends Jodie and Nina have shiny new smartphones. While walking home through the park, Paige notices a wet green $100 bill under fallen leaves. She puts the money in her pocket and imagines buying her own smartphone. Then she remembers that money is tight at home and her dad looks exhausted from working hard. Paige decides to surprise her dad instead. She takes him to a neighborhood pizza restaurant for a hot dinner. Seeing her father smile and laugh makes Paige feel proud and happy.
keySentences: Paige looked at Jodie's shiny new phone. Her friends could text and play games. (p.49)
Under a pile of wet leaves, Paige saw something green. It was a $100 bill! (p.50)
Dad smiled as the warm pizza arrived. Paige knew she had made the right choice. (p.53)

sequence: 1. Jodie and Nina show off their new smartphones at school.
2. Paige walks home through the park and spots a wet $100 bill under leaves.
3. Paige puts the money in her pocket and thinks about buying a smartphone.
4. Paige remembers money is tight at home and how tired her dad looks after work.
5. Paige takes her dad to a warm pizza restaurant and orders a meal.
6. Dad smiles happily, and Paige realizes she made the right choice.

content.clilTopic: Social Studies & History: How Money Works and Why We Save

keyFactsTeacherSaysAloud.fact: Thousands of years ago, there were no banks or coins. People bartered food and animals.
Around 600 BCE, people in Lydia made the first stamped round metal coins.
Lydia was located in Anatolia, right here in modern-day Turkey!
China invented paper money because thousands of metal coins were too heavy to carry on long trading trips.
Plastic credit cards were invented in 1958.

misconceptions.misconception: Children think credit cards give free, endless money from a magic machine.
misconceptions.clarification: A credit card is a tool to spend money that you already earned and put in a bank.

misconceptions.misconception: Children think barter is completely gone today.
misconceptions.clarification: People still barter when they trade Pokémon cards or lunch snacks at school.

realLifeLinksTurkey.link: The ancient kingdom of Lydia was located near modern Manisa and Sardis in Turkey, where the world's very first coins were minted.
Children in Turkey use a 'kumbara' (piggy bank) to save metal lira coins, exactly like the 'Save' jar on page 40.

Small desktop mat with word, emoji, and Turkish hint (e.g., 'bartered = takas etti').

challengeStronger.description: Ask stronger pupils to buy two items and calculate the total price ('$3 + $4 = $7').
Students role-play a customer who thinks an item is too expensive and asks for a discount.
Research what kind of coins the Ottoman Empire or ancient Lydia minted.

lessonSequence.title: The Coin Jars: Saving & Donating
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to identify coins and bills and ask 'How much is it?'

stages.activity: Show real coin jars labeled Save and Donate; shake jar to hear sounds.
Present Big Idea: 'Why do we need money?'; teach 'How much is it?' formula.
Classroom shop role-play with price tags ($1 to $10).
Pairs ask and answer prices of classroom stationery items.
Pupil says price of one item to leave classroom.

lessonSequence.title: Trading Before Money: The Barter Age
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to define 'barter' and explain how people traded grain and shells.

stages.activity: Quick barter game: pupils trade pencils and erasers with a desk partner.
Teach Words in Context (bartered, metal, valuable); choral read p.43.
Smartboard matching: match 6000 BCE to goats and 1200 BCE to cowrie shells.
Pupils write 2 sentences: 'People bartered grain. Shells were valuable.'
Quick oral check: 'What did ancient people trade?'

lessonSequence.title: Coins and Paper: The Heavy Money Problem
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to explain why metal coins were made in Lydia and paper money in China.

stages.activity: Hand two pupils heavy bags of stones vs a single paper bill to feel the difference.
Read pp.44-45; highlight Lydia stamped coins and Chinese paper money.
Problem-solution interactive table on smartboard.
Follow full timeline from 6000 BCE to 1958; arrange cards in order.
Thumbs up / thumbs down fact check.

lessonSequence.title: Timeline Masters: Money Review & Problem-Solution
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to complete the timeline and solve fact-check tasks.

stages.activity: Smartboard timeline drag-and-drop speed relay.
Review problem-solution relationships from text.
Pupils complete p.46 Check the Facts and p.47 graphic organizer.
Pairs present one problem and its historical solution.
Collect graphic organizer worksheets.

lessonSequence.title: The Autumn Walk: Finding the $100 Bill
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to describe the beginning of the story and understand new story words.
lessonSequence.grammar: Past simple irregular verbs (found, saw, felt).

stages.activity: Show photos of smartphones vs walking in an autumn park with leaves.
Introduce Reading 2 vocabulary; read pp.49-50 with expressive audio.
Sentence gap-fill on smartboard using the 5 new words.
Role-play: finding an object and asking 'Does this belong to you?'
Ask: 'Where did Paige find the money?'

lessonSequence.title: Paige's Dilemma: Phone vs Family
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to express moral choices using 'could' and 'should'.

stages.activity: Dilemma vote on smartboard: What would you do with $100?
Read pp.51-52; examine Paige's thoughts about her tired dad.
Could vs Should sorting game: categorize selfish vs thoughtful actions.
Pairs practice dialogue: 'She could buy a phone, but she should help Dad.'
Pupil says one 'should' sentence.

lessonSequence.title: Pizza with Dad: A Happy Choice
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to retell the climax and complete the Story Map.
lessonSequence.grammar: Past simple narrative recap (walked, found, chose, smiled).

stages.activity: Choral reading of the pizza restaurant scene (p.53).
Discuss the story moral: Why is Dad's smile worth more than a phone?
Complete p.54 Story Map (Characters, Settings, Problems, Solutions).
3-step retell with a partner using five retell starters.
Quick exit question: 'How did Paige feel at the end?'

lessonSequence.title: Phonics Workshop & Unit Showcase
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to read and write words with 'ar' and present their $100 idea.
lessonSequence.grammar: Review of price questions and past tense storytelling.

stages.activity: Tongue twister chant: 'Smart Mark parked his dark car on the farm.'
Phonics box on p.55; minimal pair contrasts (cat/cart, pack/park).
Word-sort worksheet: match pictures to 'ar' spelling words.
Mini-presentation: 'What I would do with $100' (Save, Spend, Donate).
Spell and say one 'ar' word before leaving.
